name: St Michael's Church, Váci utca
intro: The Belváros St Michael's Church stands at Váci utca 47/b in the Inner City of Pest. Its history goes back to a Dominican church in Pest in the 13th century; the present Baroque building was raised between 1700 and 1765 and later served the Pauline order and the English Ladies. Today it is a Roman Catholic church served by Premonstratensians, with an organ built by Rieger in 1892.
about: Belvárosi Szent Mihály-templom is a Roman Catholic church at Váci utca 47/b. The church's website names a church director (templomigazgató) from the Premonstratensian order, and Hungarian Wikipedia lists it under the Inner City main parish, Budapest-Belváros–Nagyboldogasszony. It is also called the church of the English Ladies (Angolkisasszonyok temploma), after the teaching order that received the building in 1787. It should not be confused with other churches of the same dedication elsewhere in Budapest.

The building is Baroque. The ceiling of the nave carries wall paintings by József Aman, and the sanctuary has a painted ceiling of its own. The organ is a Rieger instrument of 1892 with two manuals and 25 stops; its restoration began in 2007 under the organ builder Frigyes Paulus, with support that the church's website credits to the National Cultural Fund and a private donor.

This is first of all a place of worship. The Premonstratensians who serve it describe the liturgy as the centre and source of their life, and the website lists a Sunday Mass in the traditional form of the Roman rite, Masses in the ordinary form, a Greek Catholic liturgy celebrated in Ukrainian, and vespers. The church also runs a concert programme and an urn cemetery, and a choir named after Ferenc Liszt has worked here since 2004.

The church stands on Váci utca, the long pedestrian shopping street of the Inner City, and it makes a natural pairing with the Inner City Parish Church, Vörösmarty Square and the Great Market Hall. Services, concerts and the urn cemetery are managed separately, and the website carries notices about services and about visiting the crypt, so check the official page before planning a visit.
tips: Treat it as a working church: dress modestly, keep your voice low and avoid walking around during services.
Check the church's own website for services, concerts and notices, including the arrangements for the crypt, before you go.
Look up at the nave ceiling for the paintings by József Aman and find the Rieger organ; ask before photographing during a service.
Pair the visit with the Inner City Parish Church and the Great Market Hall, both in the Inner City and within walking distance.

history.intro: Its history goes back to a Dominican church in Pest in the 13th century; the building seen today is the Baroque church raised between 1700 and 1765, after the Ottoman period.

sections.heading: A Dominican beginning and a Baroque rebuilding
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia traces the church to the Dominicans, who set up a friary and church in the southern part of Pest in about 1230. After the Mongol invasion the church was moved to a new plot owned by the order, and the national assembly of 1308 that elected Charles I king is recorded as having met on that plot. The church was destroyed after the Ottoman takeover in 1541.

With the Ottomans gone, the Baroque church that stands today was built between 1700 and 1765. When Joseph II dissolved the Dominican order, the building went to the Pauline order in 1785–1786, and in 1787 it was given to the English Ladies, a teaching order.

sections.heading: Floods, fire and the Holy Right
paragraphs: Water and fire both damaged the church. It suffered in floods in 1799 and 1809, a fire in 1809 destroyed the roof and both towers, and in the great flood of 1838 the Danube stood about two metres deep inside it.
After the US Army returned the Holy Right (Szent Jobb), found in Salzburg, to Hungary in 1945, the relic was kept in this church until the English Ladies' order was dissolved in 1950.

sections.heading: Restorations from 1892 to today
paragraphs: The interior was renovated in 1892, the year of the Rieger organ. The exterior was restored in 1964–1968, when ceiling and wall paintings were whitewashed over, and again in 1997–1998. Inside, the sanctuary was restored between 1998 and 2006 and the sacristy between 2006 and 2008, and in 2012 work began on József Aman's frescoes in the nave.

sources.label: Hungarian Wikipedia: Szent Mihály-templom (Budapest V. kerület)

seo.title: St Michael's Church, Váci utca
seo.description: Baroque Roman Catholic church at Váci utca 47/b, built 1700–1765 after the Ottoman period, with an 1892 Rieger organ and Premonstratensian clergy.

name: Museum of Music History
intro: The Museum of Music History occupies the former Erdődy mansion at Táncsics Mihály utca 7 in the Castle District and belongs to the HUN-REN Institute for Musicology. Its rooms show Hungarian musical instruments, medals and badges, a memorial room for László Lajtha and a long-running exhibition inspired by Bartók, and the Baroque house also hosts concerts.
about: The museum is part of the Institute for Musicology of HUN-REN BTK. As its official pages set out its tasks, it researches the history of instruments, collects and publishes documents of Hungarian and European music history such as manuscripts, letters, pictures, instruments and legacies, and presents them in exhibitions.

The exhibitions listed on the official site include a display of musical instruments in Hungary from the mid-18th century to the 1910s, a collection of medals and badges from the early 19th to the late 20th century, a 20th-century instrument-making workshop and the workshop of the Sasvári piano hall, and a display of thirty Hungarian bows. A memorial room is devoted to the composer László Lajtha, and temporary shows have included a long-running one inspired by Bartók and one marking György Kurtág's 100th birthday.

The house has a Baroque main front two storeys high and nine bays wide, with the middle three bays projecting and an ornamented gate in the central axis. Besides the museum it holds the Institute of Musicology, the Bartók Archives and the Ernő Dohnányi Archives, and it also hosts concerts.

Táncsics Mihály utca runs through the northern part of the Castle District, close to the Vienna Gate and within walking distance of Matthias Church. The museum's page says that current exhibitions are introduced by a music historian before the concerts, so the way a visit is arranged can depend on the programme; check the official page for current arrangements and any closures.
tips: Check the museum's official page before you go: exhibitions are presented before concerts, and temporary shows have fixed end dates.
The house also hosts concerts; the museum's page links to a list of upcoming concerts.
Look up at the curved pediment of the main front, which carries the Hatvany family coat of arms.
Combine the visit with the Medieval Jewish Prayer House on the same street and the Vienna Gate at the end of it.

history.intro: The house dates from the mid-18th century, when Count György Erdődy had an earlier building demolished to make way for a new mansion; the music institute and museum are its present occupants.

sections.heading: Medieval traces and the Erdődy mansion
paragraphs: The Castle Hill history database Budavár notes that maps from the end of the Ottoman era show at least three separate properties with ruined buildings on the site. Excavations suggest that in the 14th century the land belonged to the neighbouring Kammerhof, also called the Magna Curia Regis; they uncovered the foundation walls of a polygon-ended building that was most likely part of the royal court's Saint Martin Chapel of 1349.

Count György Erdődy, who became Lord Chief Justice in 1748, acquired the land in 1743. He had the building then standing there pulled down and a stately mansion put up in its place, with work starting in 1750. The source does not name an architect.

sections.heading: Hatvany's rebuilding and the house today
paragraphs: The mansion remained essentially unchanged until 1912, when the sugar-factory owner József Hatvany bought it. His rebuilding of 1913 left only the main front as it was. The house came through the Second World War in fairly good condition and was then used as a school.

Archaeologists under Katalin H. Gyürki worked on the site between 1968 and 1976, and a modern lecture hall was subsequently built beneath the courtyard. Today the house is home to the Institute of Musicology, the Museum of Music History, the Bartók Archives and the Ernő Dohnányi Archives.

name: Fonó Budai Music House
intro: Fonó Budai Zeneház is a privately owned music house at Sztregova utca 3 in Kelenföld, south Buda. It stages jazz and world-music concerts and táncház, the Hungarian folk dance-house evenings, alongside festivals, a café and a record label, and it has been part of the capital's folk and world-music scene since it was founded in 1995.
about: The official site describes Fonó as, in the simplest sense, a communal space where people come together through music, dance and words. It hosts jazz and world-music concerts, táncház evenings and festivals, both in the house and elsewhere, and it also runs a café and rents out its rooms.

The programme listed on the Hungarian homepage includes Fonó Session, an informal community music-making evening for beginners and experienced players, and Fonó Szerda, a regular Wednesday programme. It also lists Ringató, early-years music education based on Kodály principles, and a folk music school, the Ördöngös Népzenetanoda.

A táncház is a community evening of folk dance with live music. The Táncház Association's guide describes a Fonó evening in which beginners and more experienced dancers are taught in separate groups, everyone then sings together, and the night ends with live music and free dancing; it adds that everyone is welcome with or without a partner. That listing dates from 2019, so check the current programme.

The Fonó Kávézó serves a weekday lunch menu and an à la carte menu with attention to vegetarian dishes, and the webshop sells records, including vinyl releases of the house's own label, Fonó Records. The house stands in Kelenföld, well away from the tourist centre, so it suits visitors who want an evening of live Hungarian music rather than a sight to tick off.
tips: Look at the events page on Fonó's own website for concerts and táncház evenings, and check dates and booking arrangements there.
If you have never danced a táncház, look for the evenings that include teaching for beginners; the Táncház Association's guide describes separate groups for beginners and experienced dancers.
The café is part of the house, so a meal before an evening programme is straightforward; check the café's own page for its current menu.
Kopaszi-gát and Feneketlen Lake are the nearest listed places for a walk; use a journey planner for the route to Sztregova utca, as no single line is given on the sources consulted.

history.intro: Fonó opened in 1995 as a private initiative in what the press describes as a former industrial hall, and its story is bound up with the Hungarian táncház movement.

sections.heading: A private initiative of 1995
paragraphs: A 2025 anniversary article places the opening of Fonó in 1995 and names its founder as József Lukács, a physicist by training who worked in computing. It describes the building as an empty industrial hall that had begun to decay, and says Lukács wanted a counterweight to commercialism after 1989, a small island where culture was not pre-packaged. The official site describes Fonó as a privately owned institution.

sections.heading: The táncház movement and its UNESCO recognition
paragraphs: The same article dates the first táncház to 1972, with Ferenc Novák and Ferenc Sebő among those taking part, and notes that the movement collected dances in villages across the Carpathian Basin.

In 2011 UNESCO's Intergovernmental Committee selected the Táncház method for its Register of Best Safeguarding Practices, judging it an effective way to pass folk music and dance across generations. It was not an entry on the Representative List.

sections.heading: A record label and a folk archive
paragraphs: The official site says that Fonó Records has released more than 350 albums, and it names artists associated with the house, among them György Szabados, Mihály Dresch, Félix Lajkó and Ágnes Herczku. It also credits Fonó with the Utolsó Óra (Final Hour) project, described as the largest folk music collection project at the turn of the millennium; the 2025 article puts its recordings at 23,000 melody variants and 1,250 hours of material.

name: Danube Promenade
address: Pest bank between the Széchenyi Chain Bridge and Elisabeth Bridge, Budapest V
intro: The Dunakorzó is the Pest-bank promenade between the Széchenyi Chain Bridge and Elisabeth Bridge, about a kilometre long according to Hungarian Wikipedia. It is a paved pedestrian street with views across the Danube to the Castle District, the Citadel and Gellért Hill, lined by hotels, cafés and landmarks such as the Pesti Vigadó.
about: The Dunakorzó lies on the Pest bank of the Danube in the Inner City, between the Széchenyi Chain Bridge and Elisabeth Bridge. It has been a paved pedestrian street since 1983, and Hungarian Wikipedia gives its length as about a kilometre.

The view is the point of coming. Across the water lie the Castle District, the Citadel and Gellért Hill, and Hungarian Wikipedia suggests watching the fireworks of 20 August from here. Along the way are the Pesti Vigadó, the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, Gresham Palace and, on the railing, the small bronze Little Princess statue that has sat there since 1989.

Large hotels, restaurants, cafés, bars and casinos now line the street, and tram line 2 runs along the river on a viaduct beside it. In the 19th century the same strip was the showy front yard of a row of grand hotels, and nine coffee houses operated along it.

At the southern end, on Március 15 Square beside Elisabeth Bridge, are the remains of the Roman fort Contra-Aquincum, and the Inner City Parish Church stands nearby. Hungarian Wikipedia describes the Dunakorzó as part of the Budapest World Heritage site, and BKK calls the stretch of tram line 2 between Elisabeth Bridge and the Chain Bridge a World Heritage location. BKK announced in December 2024 a tender to renew the tram viaduct and widen the stairs to the lower quay, so check BKK for the current state of the works.
tips: Walk it in either direction between the two bridges; the views of the Castle District, the Citadel and Gellért Hill face you all the way along.
Tram line 2 runs along the river here, and BKK's journey planner and news pages show current diversions or works on the viaduct.
The Little Princess statue sits on the railing and is small; if you want to photograph it, expect to share the spot with others.
Continue north to Gresham Palace and the Chain Bridge, or south to the Inner City Parish Church, to link the promenade with the rest of downtown Pest.

history.intro: The promenade grew out of the Pest embankment in the second half of the 19th century, was largely destroyed in the siege of 1945 and was remade in the decades after the war.

sections.heading: Embankment and hotel row
paragraphs: The embankment came first. Hungarian Wikipedia says the Danube Steamship Company built quay wall, 345 metres on each side of the Pest abutment of the Chain Bridge, between 1853 and 1859, although it adds that other sources give 1857 as the end date. The city of Pest then lengthened the embankment in three phases: 1857–1861, 1864–1867 and 1870–1876.

Behind the new quay rose the hotels. Grand Hotel Hungária, designed by Szkalnitzky and Koch, opened in 1871 with 302 rooms, and the promenade in front of the hotels acted as their showy forecourt, with nine coffee houses along it. The Thonet building of 1871 is the only survivor of its block.

sections.heading: 1945 and the post-war rebuilding
paragraphs: The siege of 1945 destroyed most of the major buildings on the front. Only the Bristol hotel and the Thonet building survived, while the Ritz was destroyed. The Bristol was demolished in 1969, and the Duna InterContinental, now the Marriott, was completed that year on the site of the Hungária, Bristol and Carlton hotels.
The Forum Hotel followed in 1981 on the site of the Ritz, and the Hyatt, now the Sofitel, in 1982 at Eötvös Square.

sections.heading: The tram viaduct and BKK's plans
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia gives 1896–1900 as the building period of the 498-metre tram viaduct beside the promenade. Trams began running on it in 1904 as line 16; its 16A variant was renumbered 2 in 1942, and the viaduct received monument protection in 2011.

On 23 December 2024 BKK published a conditional tender notice for renewing the viaduct between Elisabeth Bridge and the Chain Bridge, widening the stairs to the lower quay and rebuilding the track, with stricter rules because of the World Heritage status. Check BKK for the current state of the works.

name: Skanzen – Hungarian Open Air Museum
intro: Skanzen, officially the Szabadtéri Néprajzi Múzeum, is Hungary's national outdoor ethnographic museum at Sztaravodai út 75 in Szentendre. Relocated houses, churches and farm buildings are arranged as village-like regional units that show folk architecture and rural life. The museum is seasonal and closes for the winter, so check the official site for the season before travelling.
about: Skanzen sets out to show folk architecture, interiors, farming and everyday life of the Hungarian-speaking lands from the later 18th century to the earlier 20th. It does this with original houses moved here from around the country, set out on the pattern of old settlements and filled with authentic objects. The official site describes a plan to relocate more than 400 buildings, grouped into village-like regional units.

The official permanent-exhibition page speaks of nine regional units, but its list gives opening years for eight: Upper Tisza 1974, Small Plain 1987, Western Transdanubia 1993, Bakony and Balaton Uplands 2000, Southern Transdanubia 2005, Upland Market Town 2006, Northern Hungarian Village 2010 and Transylvania 2022. The Great Hungarian Plain appears on the list without an opening year. Figures for the museum's size differ between sources: the same page says 75 hectares, English Wikipedia says 63, and the museum's history page mentions 46 hectares in the Sztaravoda valley when the museum became independent in 1972.

Besides the buildings, the museum's pages describe living history in a growing number of units, daily programmes, the Skanzen train that runs through the grounds, a gastronomy section among the services, and festivals through the year.

Skanzen is in Szentendre in Pest County, not in Budapest, so it is a day trip. The official route planner gives the road journey from Budapest as roughly 40 minutes to an hour by road 11, depending on traffic. By public transport it describes taking the H5 suburban railway from Batthyány tér to Szentendre and then a local bus from the terminal to the museum.

The museum is seasonal and closes for the winter. Its pages also list homesteads and buildings in several regional units that are temporarily closed for renovation, so check the official site for the current season, special weekends and the state of the buildings.
tips: Check the official site for the season, the current programme and the list of buildings closed for renovation before you set out.
The site is large and the regional units are spread out, so plan for a lot of walking; the museum's pages also describe a Skanzen train through the grounds, to be confirmed there.
For public transport the official route planner describes the H5 suburban railway from Batthyány tér to Szentendre followed by a local bus; check the current timetable with BKK before leaving.
Seasonal festivals change the character of a visit; the programme pages list them.

history.intro: The idea of a central Hungarian skanzen is older than the museum: it grew out of a short-lived ethnographic village at the 1896 millennium exhibition, and the museum itself was founded in 1967.

sections.heading: From the 1896 Ethnographic Village to the founding decision
paragraphs: The national exhibition of 1896, marking the millennium of the Hungarian conquest, included an Ethnographic Village that the museum's history calls its most popular part. Half of it, with 24 furnished houses, a wooden church and several farm buildings, showed Hungarian rural building and life, while the other half showed the ethnic minorities. It was taken down in November 1896, but it set off research into folk architecture and the idea of a central open-air museum.

Realising that idea took almost 70 years, as doubts over the concept, a lack of money and the world wars all got in the way. A turning point came in 1949, when pieces of folk architecture were put under protection, and the surveys and research that followed built up the knowledge a central museum needed. The word skanzen itself goes back to Stockholm, where the world's first open-air museum was founded in 1891 and named after the part of town it stands in.

sections.heading: Founding in 1967 and growth by region
paragraphs: The Hungarian Open Air Museum in Szentendre was founded in 1967 as the Village Museum Department of the Budapest Ethnographical Museum and became independent in 1972. The history page adds that regional open-air museums were created elsewhere in Hungary at the same time, among them Zalaegerszeg in 1968, Szombathely in 1973 and Nyíregyháza in 1979.

In Szentendre the regional units opened one by one, starting with Upper Tisza in 1974 and most recently Transylvania in 2022. The history page, which dates from before 2010, also lists the Middle Tisza Region and the Great Hungarian Plain among the planned units; the Great Hungarian Plain now appears on the unit list without an opening year.
